title: Rotator cuff tear and impingement
text: Supraspinatus passes under the coracoacromial arch, and its tendon has a watershed of poor blood supply about 1 cm from the greater tubercle. Degenerate tears begin there. Impingement gives a painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction; a full-thickness tear gives a positive drop-arm sign and the patient shrugs to initiate abduction. Deltoid can still abduct once the arm is started, which is why a torn cuff does not abolish abduction outright.

title: Rupture of the long head of biceps
text: The long head runs in the intertubercular groove and through the shoulder joint, where it rubs and degenerates. Rupture is usually at that proximal end in an older patient, often with a pop while lifting: the muscle belly balls up distally as a Popeye sign. Elbow flexion and supination are barely weakened because the short head and brachialis take over, so it is often treated non-operatively. A distal biceps tendon rupture at the radial tuberosity is a different matter and usually needs repair.

title: Medial epicondylitis and pronator syndrome
text: Golfer's elbow is tendinosis of the common flexor origin, with pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation. Separately, the median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres, and compression there causes forearm ache with median sensory symptoms that – unlike carpal tunnel syndrome – include the palm, because the palmar cutaneous branch is caught too.

title: Trigger finger
text: A nodule on the flexor tendon catches at the A1 pulley over the metacarpal head, so the finger snaps rather than glides and may lock flexed, needing passive extension. Commonest in the ring finger and thumb, and in diabetes and rheumatoid disease. Injection or division of the A1 pulley cures it; the pulley can be sacrificed because the A2 and A4 pulleys prevent bowstringing.

title: Volkmann ischaemic contracture
text: The end point of an untreated forearm compartment syndrome, classically after a supracondylar humeral fracture. The deep flexor compartment is affected worst, so flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus fibrose and shorten: the wrist and fingers are held flexed, and the fingers extend only when the wrist is flexed. Pain on passive extension of the fingers is the early warning, long before pulses disappear.

title: Anterior compartment syndrome of the leg
text: The anterior compartment is the tightest in the leg and the commonest site after a tibial fracture or a crush. Pain out of proportion and pain on passive plantar flexion come first; paraesthesia in the first web space follows as the deep fibular nerve suffers; pulses are usually still present. Fasciotomy of all four compartments is the treatment, and waiting for a pulseless foot is waiting too long.

title: Tibialis posterior dysfunction and flat foot
text: Tibialis posterior is the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch. Attritional rupture behind the medial malleolus produces an acquired flat foot: the arch collapses, the hindfoot goes into valgus, and the patient cannot perform a single-leg heel raise. From behind, too many toes are visible lateral to the ankle.

title: Hamstring strain and avulsion
text: The commonest muscle injury in sprinting, usually at the musculotendinous junction of the long head of biceps femoris during the late swing phase, when the muscle is contracting while lengthening. A proximal avulsion of the common tendon from the ischial tuberosity gives bruising down the back of the thigh and a palpable gap, and needs surgical consideration. The sciatic nerve lies just deep to them.

title: Adductor strain and groin pain
text: Adductor longus has a small tendinous origin on the body of the pubis and takes the brunt of sudden change of direction. Tenderness at the pubic origin with pain on resisted adduction. Adductor-related groin pain overlaps with pubic-related pain, iliopsoas-related pain, inguinal-related pain and hip joint pathology, and the hip must be examined before blaming the muscle.

title: Rectus sheath haematoma
text: Rupture of the inferior epigastric vessels or of the muscle itself, after coughing, exercise or anticoagulation. A tender abdominal mass that, unlike an intra-abdominal one, stays palpable and does not cross the midline when the patient tenses the abdominal wall – Fothergill sign. Below the arcuate line there is no posterior sheath, so blood can spread freely and the swelling is larger.

title: Quadriceps and patellar tendon rupture
text: An extensor mechanism rupture leaves a straight-leg raise impossible and a palpable gap. Above 40 the tear is usually of the quadriceps tendon and the patella sits low; below 40 it is usually the patellar tendon and the patella rides high. Risk factors: steroids, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, fluoroquinolones. An X-ray showing patella alta or baja confirms the level.

title: Baker (popliteal) cyst
text: Distension of the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa, which communicates with the knee joint in about half of adults, so it usually reflects an effusion from osteoarthritis or a meniscal tear. It is felt medially in the popliteal fossa and is more prominent in extension (Foucher sign). Rupture mimics a deep vein thrombosis, with calf pain and a crescent of bruising below the malleolus.

title: Acromioclavicular joint injury
text: A fall on the point of the shoulder sprains or disrupts the acromioclavicular and then the coracoclavicular (conoid and trapezoid) ligaments. The clavicle appears to ride up; in fact the scapula and arm drop. Pain is localised to the joint and reproduced by cross-body adduction. Grades I–II are treated in a sling; higher grades, in which the coracoclavicular distance is clearly increased, may be reconstructed.

title: Clavicular fracture
text: Usually in the middle third, where the bone changes curvature and has no muscular protection. The lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the arm and the medial fragment up by sternocleidomastoid. Most unite in a sling. Watch for the rare but serious complications: injury to the subclavian vessels or the brachial plexus beneath, and a pneumothorax. It is also the last bone to fuse and the first to ossify.

title: Osteoarthritis of the hip
text: Groin pain referred to the knee by the obturator nerve, worst on weight bearing, with early loss of internal rotation and extension. Fixed flexion is unmasked by the Thomas test. Radiographs show joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, and osteophytes. Referred knee pain from the hip is a classic trap in children too, where a limp and knee pain may be a slipped upper femoral epiphysis.

title: The swollen knee: what the timing tells you
text: Immediate swelling (within an hour) means blood: an anterior cruciate rupture, a peripheral meniscal tear, a patellar dislocation or an osteochondral fracture. Swelling overnight means a reactive effusion, typically a meniscal tear or arthritis. Blood with fat globules means an intra-articular fracture. A hot, exquisitely painful knee that the patient will not move is a septic joint until aspirated.

title: Inversion ankle sprain
text: The commonest ligament injury in the body. The anterior talofibular ligament tears first, then the calcaneofibular, then the posterior talofibular. Ottawa rules: X-ray only if there is bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, at the navicular or at the base of the fifth metatarsal, or if the patient cannot bear weight for four steps. Always examine the proximal fibula for a Maisonneuve fracture.

title: Temporomandibular joint dislocation
text: The condyle slips forward over the articular eminence, usually on wide opening, and spasm of the masseter and temporalis holds it there. The mouth is stuck open and the jaw protruded. Reduction is by downward and backward pressure on the lower molars with the thumbs, protected: the muscles snap the jaw shut sharply as it relocates.

title: Muscles of mastication and V3
text: Masseter, temporalis and the pterygoids are all supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Wasting of temporalis hollows the temple and is visible before it is measurable. A unilateral V3 lesion deviates the jaw towards the weak side on opening, because the intact lateral pterygoid pushes the condyle forward unopposed. Temporalis is also the muscle of the temporalis flap used in head and neck reconstruction.

title: Torticollis and the accessory nerve
text: Congenital muscular torticollis is fibrosis of one sternocleidomastoid, tilting the head towards the affected side and rotating the chin away; it is associated with birth trauma and with plagiocephaly. The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and is very superficial in the posterior triangle, where lymph node biopsy can divide it – leaving a drooping shoulder, a weak shrug and difficulty abducting above the horizontal.

title: Thoracic outlet syndrome
text: The lower trunk of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery pass between scalenus anterior and medius over the first rib. A cervical rib, a fibrous band or hypertrophied scalenes compress them. Neurogenic cases (the great majority) give wasting of the thenar eminence and C8–T1 sensory loss; vascular cases give a cold, pale arm with a reduced pulse on abduction, and can throw emboli to the hand.

title: Diaphragmatic injury and hernia
text: Blunt trauma ruptures the left hemidiaphragm far more often than the right, which is shielded by the liver, and bowel then herniates into the chest – bowel gas above the diaphragm or a nasogastric tube seen in the left hemithorax. Congenitally, a posterolateral Bochdalek defect lets abdominal viscera into the chest and causes pulmonary hypoplasia; an anterior Morgagni hernia is rarer and usually right-sided.

title: Pelvic floor injury and prolapse
text: Vaginal delivery can avulse levator ani from the pubic bone or stretch the pudendal nerve. The result is loss of the hammock supporting the urethra and pelvic organs: stress incontinence, cystocele, rectocele and uterine prolapse. Pelvic floor muscle training works because levator ani is skeletal muscle under voluntary control, unlike the internal sphincters.

title: Mechanical back pain and the erector spinae plane block
text: Most acute back pain is musculoligamentous and self-limiting; red flags are what matter – age under 20 or over 55, night pain, weight loss, fever, trauma, steroid use, neurological deficit or sphincter disturbance. The erector spinae plane block, injecting local anaesthetic deep to the muscle against the transverse process, has become a common alternative to a paravertebral block for rib fractures and thoracic surgery.

title: Quadratus lumborum and the twelfth rib
text: Quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest to the twelfth rib and the lumbar transverse processes, fixing the rib during inspiration. The subcostal nerve and the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves cross its front, which is why a loin incision or a QL block affects sensation over the groin. It lies directly behind the kidney, which is why loin pain and a psoas or quadratus spasm can be hard to tell apart.

title: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome
text: Lateral hip pain, worse lying on that side and on climbing stairs, caused by tendinopathy or a tear of gluteus medius and minimus at the greater trochanter, with or without bursitis. Tenderness is over the trochanter, and a 30-second single-leg stance reproduces it. Because the same muscles are the hip abductors, a chronic tear produces a Trendelenburg gait.

title: The calf pump and deep vein thrombosis
text: Soleus contains large venous sinuses, and calf muscle contraction is the main pump returning blood from the leg. Immobility removes that pump, which is why long flights, plaster casts and bed rest cause deep vein thrombosis, and why early mobilisation and calf compression prevent it. Most calf thrombi start in the soleal veins.

title: Deltoid injection and axillary nerve injury
text: The axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck of the humerus about 5–7 cm below the acromion, so an intramuscular injection must be given in the upper third of the deltoid. The nerve is injured by anterior shoulder dislocation, by a surgical neck fracture and by badly placed injections: the patient loses abduction beyond the first 15 degrees and has numbness over the regimental badge area.

title: Latissimus dorsi as a flap
text: Latissimus dorsi has a single dominant pedicle, the thoracodorsal artery, which lets the whole muscle be raised and swung on that vessel – the workhorse flap for breast reconstruction and for covering large defects. The thoracodorsal nerve runs with the artery along the posterior axillary wall and is at risk in axillary clearance, leaving a weak adducted, internally rotated pull ('the handcuff muscle').

title: Trapezius palsy after neck surgery
text: Trapezius is supplied by the accessory nerve, which crosses the posterior triangle with almost no protection. Division during lymph node biopsy or neck dissection causes shoulder droop, a dull ache, an inability to shrug, and winging that is worse on abduction (unlike serratus anterior palsy, where winging is worse on forward pushing).

title: Vastus medialis and knee extension
text: The lowest, more horizontal fibres of vastus medialis insert into the medial border of the patella and resist lateral tracking. It wastes quickly after any knee injury or effusion – within days – and is the first thing to look for and the first thing to rehabilitate. Loss of the last 10–15 degrees of extension (an extension lag) is the functional consequence.

title: Scaphoid fracture
text: A fall on the outstretched hand with tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and on telescoping the thumb. The blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde, so a proximal fracture risks avascular necrosis and non-union. Initial radiographs miss up to a quarter of fractures: immobilise and re-image, or go to MRI. Untreated it leads to scaphoid non-union advanced collapse of the wrist.
